title: Raéyn — Mistress of the Sea
subtitle: Tides & Change

lore.description:
She arrives. That is the first thing and most of the rest of it.

A morning of flat silver, gulls sitting on the water, and then a line on the horizon the color of a bruise, and then the line is a wall, and then the wall is over you and the noise is such that men standing a yard apart cannot make each other understand a single word. Four hours later there is sun on the wet deck and the sea is the color of milk and glass and someone is laughing, which is the part outsiders never believe.

Raéyn is not a kind mother and has never once claimed to be. She is enormous, she is free, and she is in a mood — and the mood is not about you, which is the hardest thing about her for people who want the world to be about them. She is called Storm-Queen in Kahfagia, Tide-Mother in Linn, Salt-Widow on the Brass Coast, and she answers to all of it and to none of it and to whistling, sometimes, which is why nobody whistles.

She favors those who read a current, bargain with weather, and go anyway. She is fiercely protective of them and will not be relied upon, and both of those are permanently true at the same time.

Her son is Khemesh. She does not speak of him and the sea does not stop being one water.

**The Storm-Queen at the harbor mouth.**

Kahfagian shipowners commission Raéyn with a crown high enough to be seen from the channel. Crews leave smaller images where a wet hand can reach them on departure. Both offer thanks after a ship returns, but they remember different things: the owner names the vessel and its venture; the shore household names the person who stepped from it. At some harbor feasts the two lists are read separately, an arrangement established after quarrels about which returns deserved celebration.

Her worship traveled with pilots and migrant crews before any harbor authority tried to regularize it. A shrine may hold stones from several home shores, each brought by someone who survived a crossing. Expanding a quay can require moving that shrine. The engineer may be a devotee too, and know exactly why the pilots object to a new entrance facing a different current.

**The Tide-Mother and the Salt-Widow.**

Among the Linn, a returning crew shares its first shore meal with the households that waited. The Tide-Mother receives a portion beside people who have recovered someone and people who have not. No priest can make those groups feel the same thing. A singer who praises Raéyn's protection too confidently may be interrupted by a parent asking for the name left out of the song.

On the Brass Coast, the Salt-Widow's observances developed around households left to settle unfinished voyages. Her attendants know which captain promised to bring a person home and which relative has heard nothing except that the ship was sold. They sit through inventories and disputes as readily as prayers. This is the Brass Coast of the Amaranthine; the Bronze Coast's Sidhi lighthouse traditions have their own history and are not a second name for this cult.

**The Mother of the Returning Sail.**

In some Nihori fishing ports, Raéyn is the Mother of the Returning Sail. Rescue crews keep her at a shore shrine beside the gear used to bring boats through dangerous water. The title became common as households from different islands shared a landing after storms destroyed their former harbors. Their shrine accounts preserve the names of the rescuers as well as the rescued. A local kami may receive an offering there without being declared another form of Raéyn.

These houses emphasize her fierce protection. Pilots from Kahfagia sometimes accuse them of making her too dependable; the port attendants answer by pointing to equipment still being repaired. Asking protection is compatible with knowing it may not arrive. Her son remains Khemesh. A cup for a missing sailor does not turn his depths into a kindly ancestral hall, and a returned body does not prove that every disappearance was his doing.
lore.followers: Among the peoples of Fate's Edge, Raéyn is called by many names. In Kahfagia, she is the Storm-Queen; in Linn, the Tide-Mother; in the Brass Coast, the Salt-Widow. Her cult is syncretic, blending the fierce protectiveness of a mother goddess with the practical cunning of a harbor master.
signs: A sudden shift in the wind that favours your course
A wave that rises higher than the rest, then calms
The smell of salt water on a windless day
quotes: "Mark the tide, name your course, and trust the wave-road. But speak ill of Khemesh, and even I may let the deep take you."
"The sea does not hate you. It tests you. Pass, and the waves remember your name."
"The sea gives, the sea takes. We who love her learn to swim."

domain_focus: Tides and Currents: change, opportunity, the rhythm of the sea
Maritime Trade and Travel: safe passage, navigation, weather
Storm and Calm: the duality of protection and wrath
Motherhood and Loss: fierce love, grief for Khemesh, the weight of a divided heart

thiasos.description: Raéyn's Thiasos is a small sea creature or mythological being of the waves: a storm petrel that appears before gales and can sense pressure drops, a gray seal pup that sings in harmonic tones audible only underwater, a hermit crab whose shell is etched with wave-runes, a small octopus that changes color to reflect the weather, or a sea horse that can hover in still air for a heartbeat.
thiasos.care: Beyond its ordinary care, this Thiasos must be immersed in salt water (or exposed to sea spray) each day. If kept dry for more than a day, it becomes Compromised (it grows listless and its color fades; its bearer loses the benefit of Sailor's Instinct until it is returned to the sea).

codex.description: Raéyn keeps no Codex that resembles a book of dry paper. It may be a set of tide charts etched on whalebone, a bundle of knotted cords that record the phases of the moon and the turn of currents, a conch shell whose interior spiral is inscribed with navigational verse, or a driftwood plank carved with wave-runes that only become visible when wet.
codex.upkeep: Because the sea resists being fixed in writing, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week soaking it in salt water or tracing its symbols by the light of a tide pool, or the Rites stored there become faint (treat as Compromised until re-consecrated at the shore).

patrons_gift.name: Promise of Safe Passage
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of Raéyn may touch a held item (weapon, tool, or piece of gear) and whisper a promise of safe passage.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Navigation or Athletics rolls when aboard a vessel or in water, and the first time each scene the bearer would suffer an environmental penalty from rough seas, wind, or rain, they may ignore it.
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to Raéyn.

rites.name: Rite of the Wave-Tide
rites.materials: A knotted length of salt-twine brushed with seawater, or a shell held to the ear while facing the wind.
rites.effect: Choose one: (a) Tidemark's Blessing: Treat slick, swaying, or water-slicked footing as stable for this scene. Gain +1 die on boarding, balance, or shipboard movement. Create a 4-segment Tide's Favor timer to ignore one level of difficult terrain. (b) Whispering Currents: Learn the safest near-term route across water or coastline, or gain +1 die to navigation checks for this scene. If Khemesh's influence is present, suffer –1 die from conflicting currents.
rites.push_it: (Tidemark) Extend to one ally in Close for one beat, but generate 1 SB (Spades) as the deck shifts. (Currents) Also learn the fastest route, but mark Exposure +1 (leaving a telltale wake). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Changing Tide
rites.materials: A handful of pebbles cast in a crescent.
rites.effect: Bias currents and water levels in the zone (must be water-adjacent). Those moving with the tide gain +1 die; those moving against suffer –1 die. Small craft must test to hold position. Create a 6-segment Tidal Influence timer.
rites.push_it: Brief surge or drawdown (one beat): open a ford or swamp a skiff. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Wave-Road Consecration
rites.materials: Two sea glass markers dropped overboard at start and end.
rites.effect: Consecrate a wave-road between two visible points. Allies gain +2 dice on travel, evade, or carry actions at sea. Designated pursuers suffer –1 die to intercept. One active wave-road at a time. Create an 8-segment Blessed Passage timer.
rites.push_it: Extend the route's favor to an adjacent leg for one beat; mark +1 Obligation. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Storm-Queen's Hand
rites.materials: A vial of rainwater gathered at three crossings.
rites.effect: Shape a storm-band over the zone (sea, shore, or open sky). Choose two modes at cast; switch one once per scene: (a) Propulsion: Vessel gains +1 band of movement per beat (or +1 Effect to maneuvers). (b) Concealment: Veil of rain/spray; ranged targeting impaired; –1 die to hostile sighting. (c) Smite: Once per beat, lash with wave or lightning as [AREA] hazard.
rites.push_it: Add a third mode for one beat, then the GM spends 1 SB on collateral. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Mother's Wrath
rites.materials: Tears of a betrayed lover mixed with salt from seven seas.
rites.effect: Curse those who wronged you. The target suffers –2 dice to maritime/weather rolls for one session. At sea, they must roll Spirit+Endurance (DV 4) each day or suffer Harm 1 (Weather). Create a 6-segment Mother's Ire timer.
rites.push_it: The curse spreads to the target's allies or family; mark 2 SB (Diamonds). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of Raéyn sings in shanties of the turning tide—melodies that rise and fall with the rhythm of waves, harmonies that mimic the creak of rigging and the cry of gulls. Their voice is used to calm a restless sea, to call a favorable wind, or to sing a drowned sailor's soul back to shore. Raéyn's Cantors are often found aboard ships, their songs becoming part of the vessel's luck.

cult.name: The Cult of the Salt-Washed Circle
cult.description: Raéyn's cults gather on beaches at low tide, in sea caves, and aboard ships during storms. The Salt-Washed Circle is a fellowship of sailors, pilots, fisherfolk, and coastal dwellers who honor the sea's gifts and respect its rages. A ritual of the Circle involves each member pouring a libation of fresh water into the sea (to honor Raéyn's tears for Khemesh) while speaking a wish for safe passage or a warning of danger ahead. Their creed is carved into driftwood and left on the tide: 'The sea gives, the sea takes. We who love her learn to swim.' Outsiders are welcome to join a libation, but they must bring salt from their home shore.

witchcraft.name: The Art of the Tide
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with Raéyn is a net mender or tide-seer—one who crafts with the materials of the tide: a hull carved from wood seasoned by sea salt, a sail woven with a prayer for fair wind, or a net tied with knots that remember every fish they have caught. In Aeler, a True-Mason might carve a 'tide stone' at a harbor entrance, but a witch of Raéyn would instead tie a salt-twine knot around a piling, so that the current remembers to favor outgoing vessels.
witchcraft.lore: The tide-seer's path is the art of reading the sea. They learn that the tide does not ask permission—it simply moves. To serve Raéyn is to understand that change is the only constant, and that the sea rewards those who respect its rhythm.
witchcraft.quote: Mark the tide, name your course, and trust the wave-road.

wave_seer_shell.name: The Wave-Seer's Shell
wave_seer_shell.description: A large conch shell, its inner spiral polished to a mirror sheen, rimmed with brass. Once per session, the witch may hold the shell to their ear and listen to the 'tide's memory.' For the next scene, they gain +2 dice to navigation or weather-reading rolls, and may ask the GM one yes/no question about hidden currents, reefs, or approaching storms (the shell whispers the answer in a voice like waves). The shell can also be used to 'mark' a threshold: placing it on a ship's prow or a harbor gate grants +1 die to all rolls made to defend that vessel or harbor until the next dawn.

hedge_gifts.name: Salt-Kissed Rope
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, the witch may tie a simple knot in a rope, cord, or strand of hair while speaking a short prayer to Raéyn. The knot becomes a tide-knot—when the witch unties it (as a free action), the nearest body of water (a puddle, a river, the sea) briefly rises or falls by a few inches, as if a small tide has turned. This can unstick a boat, wet a fire, or startle a guard—but never causes direct harm.

hedge_gifts.name: The Mariner's Compass
hedge_gifts.description: Once per voyage (or per session, if not at sea), you may ask the GM one yes/no question about the weather or the state of the sea for the next 24 hours. The GM must answer truthfully.

hedge_gifts.name: The Drowned Sailor's Blessing
hedge_gifts.description: When you or an ally falls overboard, you may call on Raéyn. The water will bear you up for one exchange, granting +2 dice to any check to climb back aboard or swim to safety.

monastic_tradition.name: The Way of the Storm Pilot
monastic_tradition.description: The sea does not hate you. It tests you. Pass, and the waves remember your name. Storm Pilots understand that the sea is not an enemy—it is a teacher. They read currents, bargain with weather, and carry news between shores. To walk this path is to accept that the tide that lifts you can also drag you down, and that the only way to master the sea is to respect its power.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Wits 3+, Spirit 2+, Rite of the Wave-Tide or Cantor of Raéyn.
monastic_tradition.quote: The sea does not hate you. It tests you. Pass, and the waves remember your name.
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: The sea's debts are tides, not chains. Monks of the Storm Pilot tradition gain +1 die to resist any magical debt or geas that would bind them to a fixed port or restrict their freedom to sail. If they succeed, the contract's ink runs like water and the obligation washes away.

basic.name: Sea Legs
basic.effect: You ignore all penalties from rough seas or slippery decks.

advanced.name: Call the Breeze
advanced.effect: Once per scene, increase your vessel's speed by one band for one exchange.

master.name: Eye of the Storm
master.effect: Once per session, you may calm a supernatural storm or redirect a natural one for one scene. All weather-based penalties are negated for your vessel and allies within Near.
master.cost: After the scene, you gain a permanent Storm-Touched Eye (one iris glimmers with distant lightning, and the sea will occasionally call you to calm another tempest). You may ignore one Obligation to Raéyn, but the next natural storm you encounter will find you regardless of shelter.

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Sailor's Instinct: +1 die to Navigation and maritime survival rolls.
corruption.cost: Sea-Sick on Land: –1 die to rolls requiring prolonged time away from water or open spaces.

corruption.benefit: Tide's Favor: Once/scene, treat a failed maritime or weather-related roll as a success, but mark 1 SB (Clubs).
corruption.cost: Weather Sensitive: Must make a Resolve test (DV 3) to resist acting on every weather change or maritime opportunity.

corruption.benefit: Storm's Child: +2 dice to rolls involving weather manipulation or sea-based combat.
corruption.cost: Tempestuous Nature: Suffer 1 Fatigue when denied access to open water or weather changes for extended periods.

corruption.benefit: Mother's Protection: Once/session, call upon Raéyn's favor to protect a vessel or coastal area from harm.
corruption.cost: Protective Instinct: –1 die to rolls involving personal safety when others are endangered nearby.

corruption.benefit: Wave-Rider: Once/session, navigate any water-based obstacle or hazard with perfect ease.
corruption.cost: Restless Spirit: –1 die to rolls requiring patience or stillness; the call of the sea is constant.

corruption.benefit: Storm Queen: Once/session, become the living embodiment of the sea's power. For one scene, control weather and tides within Near range.
corruption.cost: Mother's Burden: Mark +2 Obligation when using this power; the weight of protecting all who sail becomes overwhelming, causing Harm 1 (Stress) until the storm passes. Khemesh's Attention: The Kraken's gaze turns your way; the GM may introduce oceanic complications (rogue waves, crushing pressure) as narrative fallout.

playstyle_notes.description:
Raéyn is for a character who wants motion, weather, and the freedom of not being owed anything — and who can live with a patron whose favor is real, immense, and not dependable. She does not withdraw her blessing to punish; she is simply otherwise engaged, at scale, and the consequences of that arrive at full size.

Play her in weather rather than in words. Her attention should be felt as barometric before it is felt as narrative — the light going wrong, the gulls inland, the temperature dropping in a closed room. When she is pleased, it is glorious and slightly too much. Her rivalry with Khemesh is the whole architecture of the sea: she is what the water does, he is what it weighs.
emphasizes: Tides and Change: power over currents, weather, and the rhythm of the sea
Maritime Syncretism: a goddess of creole Kahfagia, blending mother, warrior, and storm
Storm and Calm: the duality of protection and wrath
Motherhood and Loss: fierce love for sailors, grief for Khemesh
Khemesh's Shadow: the Kraken is always beneath the waves, watching

sample_adventure.title: The Kraken's Wake
sample_adventure.description: Merchant ships are disappearing in the Sea of Thorns. Survivors describe a vast shape below their hulls and a pressure that silences the rigging before it breaks. A kraken marked by Khemesh has settled across the shipping route. Raéyn's followers can read the currents around its hunting ground, but cannot promise calm water there. The party must divert the fleet, draw the creature away, or risk a crossing before the ports run short of grain.
sample_adventure.quote: Mark the tide, name your course, and trust the wave-road. But speak ill of Khemesh, and even I may let the deep take you.

guises.name: The Tide-Mother
guises.note: She is carved with a boat held against her ribs, its occupants too small to distinguish. Boat families hang patched mittens beside the image, including those belonging to people brought home dead. The same hymn can accompany a launch and a burial. A captain who calls survival proof of her affection is likely to be corrected by someone preparing the second ceremony.

guises.name: The Storm-Queen
guises.note: Shipping houses prefer a crowned figure above the harbor chain. Their gifts commemorate named rescues and voyages; dockside shrines often remove the donors' painted arms when salt has eaten through them. Pilots ask for passage. House chaplains sometimes speak as though the sea has recognized an exclusive charter. The pilots rarely repeat that language outside the breakwater.

guises.among: The Brass Coast of the Amaranthine
guises.name: The Salt-Widow
guises.note: Her veil is made from sailcloth and replaced by the households that washed the last one. Services count the returned separately from the missing, leaving room for a boat to come in after its funeral. This is the Brass Coast observance; it should not be relocated to Dhahara's Bronze Coast because the names sound alike.

guises.name: The Lady Who Brings the Boat Within Sight
guises.note: A painted sea-lady stands beside wooden models of rescued craft. Coastal families brought the image home from foreign ports; local keepers adopted it into rites for safe return while retaining their own ancestors and shore spirits. Inland catalogues identify her with Raéyn more confidently than the keepers do. A family may use her imported name abroad and its harbor title at home.

guises.name: The Guest Beyond the Breakwater
guises.note: A place is left for her at a launch feast, facing outward. The shrine attends to the local kami before addressing the sea beyond their accustomed waters. Some crews treat Raéyn as a visiting sovereign; others as an unwelcome relative whom good manners may persuade to pass by. Neither makes her subject to a daimyo's permission.

provenance.origin: Her cult has many shores and no agreed first landing.
provenance.summary: Linn singers say their grandmothers heard her before foreign ships possessed sails. Kahfagian temple histories begin with a rescued harbor founder. Sailcloth images on the Brass Coast preserve neither story intact. Raéyn has acquired crowns, veils, and maternal titles without becoming as consistent as any of them. A calm image beside a quay can represent a power whose next approach strips that quay bare.
provenance.the_migration: Worship travels with pilots, rescued passengers, and the families of sailors who marry ashore. A household first hangs an unfamiliar image in thanks; a neighboring crew borrows its departure song; a prosperous sponsor builds a roof over the place. Only later does a priest arrive to explain which parts have been performed incorrectly. The Salt-Washed Circle carries practices between these shrines without settling their precedence.
provenance.why_it_took: Harbor authorities value a cult that can make rival crews share a service before they must share a channel. Its keepers also speak for the families left waiting. In some ports the memorial procession is permitted on the quay but forbidden to stop outside the shipping houses. There the argument about where to carry the image has become an argument about responsibility for a lost vessel.
provenance.note: Khemesh remains her son. Regional hymns omit, lament, or refuse that relationship; their silence does not turn him into an unrelated sea monster, and his hunger must not be assigned to every local tide spirit.

philosophy.name: What Comes Back
philosophy.summary: The sea can return somebody without being kind to them. Raéyn's protectiveness is real and unreliable, and a rescue does not purchase a predictable next voyage.
philosophy.the_point: A household may love her for the same intervention another household mourns. A changed current brings one boat into shelter and sends wreckage from another past its door. The dispute cannot be solved by announcing that both gifts were equally welcome.
philosophy.the_third_thing: The Salt-Washed have to decide whether gratitude permits a public complaint. Those who cannot speak of what was lost eventually find that only successful captains are heard at the shrine.
philosophy.at_the_table: Use a returned ship whose captain wants a triumphal service while its missing crew's families want their names spoken first. A new omen can make departure urgent without telling anyone which account Raéyn prefers.
